DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review of "Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection" (Thornbury District Council)

The pilot is useful evidence and most of the arithmetic is correct. But three of the study's central claims are contradicted by its own figures:

1. Participation was not similar across houses and flats.
2. Treatment capacity at Brookfield covers only about two-thirds of the projected tonnage.
3. Once the participation figure is corrected, the service is no longer fully funded.

**Figures that check out:**
- **Table 1 percentages:** 2,112/3,200 = 66%; 168/800 = 21%; 2,280/4,000 = 57%.
- **Vehicle cost:** 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400.
- **Crew cost:** 12 × £34,000 = £408,000.
- **Total cost:** £733,400.
- **Saving:** £74 per tonne × 3,290 t = £243,000.
- **Net cost:** £490,400.
- **Pilot representativeness:** the pilot's share of flats (20%) matches the district's. That is a real strength, and it is what makes the pilot results directly usable for district-wide projections.

## 1. Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**. The text says participation was "broadly similar across housing types", and the conclusion of a single uniform service rests on that claim. The data say the opposite: the service as piloted largely failed in flats.

This is the most consequential error in the study. About 10,400 of the district's households are flats. Most councils find flats need a different design, such as communal food-waste bins at bin stores, door-knocking and different caddy arrangements. Those cost money and are not in Table 2. The recommendation should be a service with a **separate approach for flats**, costed.

## 2. The projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies a **64%** participation rate, but the pilot measured **57%**. Because the district has the same share of flats as the pilot, 57% applies directly. Projected by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg per week | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | about 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | about 160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **about 2,870** |

The figure of 3,290 tonnes is overstated by about 13%.

Two caveats on the corrected figure:
- **Season.** The pilot ran from January to June, so it misses summer and autumn, when food waste volumes differ.
- **Novelty.** Participation in pilots often falls once the novelty wears off.

The 2,870 tonnes is therefore an estimate, not a firm figure.

## 3. Brookfield cannot take most of the waste until 2029

Brookfield's contracted capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year** until its expansion. Even the corrected projection exceeds that by about **1,070 tonnes**, and the study's own figure exceeds it by about 1,490.

The next plant is **46 miles away**. The study gives no gate fee for it, no haulage or transfer cost, and no extra vehicle time. The £74-per-tonne saving is therefore available on only 1,800 tonnes, and the remainder has an unknown cost. The author's description, "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away", is true for only part of the waste.

**What would settle it:** a quote for the remaining tonnage, including transport, for 2027–29, and a firm date for the Brookfield expansion.

## 4. "Fully funded" doesn't hold

With the corrected tonnage, the disposal saving falls to about **£212,500** (2,870 × £74). Net cost becomes:

£733,400 − £212,500 = **about £521,000**

That is already above the **provisional** £520,000 allocation, *before* adding:
- the cost of treating and hauling the waste Brookfield can't take (§3);
- a separate service for flats (§1);
- costs not shown in Table 2, below.

**Costs that appear to be missing.** The author describes the cost list as complete, but it seems to leave out:
- **Staff on-costs.** Is £34,000 a salary, or the full cost including employer NI and pension? On-costs typically add 25–30%.
- **Relief staff** to cover crew holiday and sickness.
- **Supervision and administration.**
- **The dedicated phone line and web page.**
- **The cost of financing the vehicles**, beyond straight-line depreciation.
- **Liners after the first three months**, if the Council continues to supply them. Say whether the £88,000 includes ongoing liners.
- **Depot space** for six extra vehicles.

On funding: the allocation is provisional and the Government "has indicated" it. That is a reasonable planning assumption, but it should be presented as a risk, not as full coverage.

A realistic net cost is probably **well above £520,000**. The study should present a range and say how any gap would be met.

## 5. The legal deadline may already have passed

Section 1 notes that weekly food waste collections are required. Under the Simpler Recycling rules, the deadline for most English councils was **31 March 2026**, with transitional arrangements for some councils with existing contracts. A start date of April 2027 may mean Thornbury is already out of compliance.

This doesn't weaken the case for the service. It changes the decision: Cabinet is choosing *how* and *how fast*, not *whether*. The study should state Thornbury's position, whether it has a transitional arrangement and until when, so that Cabinet weighs any delay correctly.

## 6. The timetable has two risks the study doesn't address

- **Vehicles.** Ordering in December for March delivery assumes a three-month lead time. Lead times for specialist collection vehicles have often been much longer. Get written confirmation from the supplier before relying on it.
- **Crews.** Recruiting from February leaves about two months to hire **six HGV drivers** plus six loaders, and train them, before collections start. Driver shortages make that tight. Recruiting earlier, or arranging agency cover, would reduce the risk.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Satisfaction.** The 81% figure is from "surveyed pilot households". Give the response rate. Non-participants, including most flats, are less likely to respond, so the figure probably overstates satisfaction across all households.
- **Yield per household.** The overall yield of 1.9 kg is the houses figure rounded. The weighted average is 1.86 kg. This is minor, but use the split figures in projections.
- **Contamination.** Under 2% in spot checks is good. Say how many checks were made.

## What should go to Cabinet

1. **Approve the vehicle order now.** Given the legal duty and the lead time, delaying it only makes the timetable worse. The six-vehicle fleet is sized by number of households, so the tonnage correction doesn't change it.
2. **Do not approve the service as "uniform and fully funded".** Ask for a revised paper with:
   - corrected tonnage (about 2,870 t, as a range);
   - a costed approach for flats;
   - a treatment and haulage solution for the roughly 1,100 t above Brookfield's capacity until 2029;
   - the missing cost lines;
   - a funding position that shows any gap and how it would be met.
3. **State the Council's compliance position** against the statutory deadline.

The pilot's real findings are good participation and low contamination in houses, high satisfaction among respondents, and a representative mix of wards. They support going ahead. They don't support the claims that the service is uniform, local and fully funded.
